title: Understanding Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Causes, Symptoms, Complications, and Prevention | Fact-File
abstract:
## I. What Is Diabetes Mellitus?  
Diabetes mellitus is a group of metabolic disorders characterized by persistent hyperglycemia, or elevated blood glucose levels. It occurs either because the pancreas does not produce enough insulin (a hormone that regulates blood sugar), or because the body’s cells do not respond properly to insulin, or both. The name “diabetes mellitus” is derived from Greek and Latin origins: “diabetes” means “siphon” (referring to frequent urination), and “mellitus” means “sweet” (due to the presence of sugar in the urine).  
Glucose is the body’s primary source of energy and is derived from the food we eat. Insulin, produced by the beta cells of the pancreas, helps cells absorb glucose for energy. When this process fails, glucose accumulates in the blood, leading to the array of health issues we [associate with diabetes](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/diabetes).

## VI. Diabetes Management  
As we talk about Understanding Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Causes, Symptoms, Complications, and Prevention. Managing diabetes involves a combination of lifestyle changes, regular monitoring, and medications. The exact approach varies by type and individual circumstances.  
1. Blood Glucose Monitoring  
Regular monitoring helps keep glucose levels within target ranges. This can be done using:  
1. Glucometers (finger-prick devices)
2. Continuous glucose monitors (CGMs)
3. Medications
4. Type 1 Diabetes: Requires insulin therapy.
5. Type 2 Diabetes: May include oral hypoglycemic agents (e.g., metformin, sulfonylureas), GLP-1 receptor agonists, or insulin.
6. Gestational Diabetes: Managed with diet and, if needed, insulin.
7. Nutritional Therapy  
Working with a registered dietitian can help develop an individualized meal plan that balances carbohydrate intake and overall nutrition.  
1. Physical Activity  
Exercise not only helps control weight but also lowers blood glucose levels and improves heart health.  
1. Stress Management  
Stress can affect blood sugar control. Techniques such as mindfulness, yoga, and cognitive behavioral therapy can be beneficial.
